notes.b: Water on its own is poor at cleaning greasy things, because water and oil do not mix. A surfactant is the kind of substance that fixes this, and soap is the best-known example.
points: A surfactant (surface-active agent) is a substance whose molecules or ions have a water-attracting (hydrophilic) part and a water-repelling (hydrophobic) part, so one particle can interact with both water and oil.
Dissolved in water, a surfactant lowers the surface tension (the pull between surface water molecules that makes water bead up), which helps water wet surfaces and mix with oil and grease.
Soap is a surfactant: the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid, called a fatty acid (an acid with a long hydrocarbon chain ending in –COOH).
Sodium stearate, C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻Na⁺, is sodium octadecanoate, a typical soap.
Potassium soaps are softer and are used in liquid soaps.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts of a surfactant. The head is hydrophilic and the tail is hydrophobic, so don't reverse them.

notes.b: A soap ion has two ends with opposite attitudes to water. This split personality is what lets soap clean, and it is the basis of any question on how soap works.
points: The head, the carboxylate group –COO⁻, is ionic and hydrophilic: it is attracted to polar water molecules (molecules with slightly positive and negative ends) by ion–dipole attraction, and so dissolves in water.

The tail is a long hydrocarbon chain of about 12–18 carbon atoms; it is non-polar and hydrophobic, so it does not mix with water but dissolves in grease and oil through London dispersion forces (weak attractions between non-polar molecules).
This dual nature lets one soap ion interact with both water and grease.
Soap can dissolve the non-polar oils on skin, and through its ionic heads and the water it also removes the salts in sweat.
Diagram: a soap ion drawn as a long zig-zag tail, with a circled –COO⁻ head and a separate Na⁺ ion, labelled hydrophobic tail and hydrophilic head.
notes.tip: A common exam question asks how soap can dissolve both the oils and the salts in sweat. Answer with the structure: the tail takes the oils and the ionic head with the water takes the salts.

notes.b: Grease holds dirt to skin and fabric, and plain water cannot lift it. Soap works in a fixed sequence, ending with the grease trapped in tiny spheres that rinse away.
points: 1. In water, soap lowers the surface tension, so the water spreads over and wets the greasy surface or fabric instead of beading up.
2. The hydrophobic tails dissolve in the grease or oil, while the hydrophilic heads stay in the water at the surface of the grease.
3. Rubbing or agitation breaks the grease into tiny droplets, each surrounded by soap ions.
4. Each droplet becomes a micelle: a sphere with the grease and the tails inside, and the negatively charged heads facing out into the water.

5. The negative surfaces of the micelles repel one another, so the droplets do not join up again and stay dispersed in the water as an emulsion (tiny droplets of one liquid spread through another); this is emulsification.
6. Rinsing carries the micelles away, with the dirt and microorganisms trapped in the grease.
Diagram: a micelle, with an oil droplet in the centre, soap tails pointing inward into it, and heads (–COO⁻) on the outside in water.
notes.tip: In a micelle the tails point inward into the grease and the heads point outward into the water. Soap does not simply dissolve grease in water; it emulsifies it into micelles that are rinsed away. A full answer uses the terms hydrophilic, hydrophobic and micelle and includes a labelled diagram.

notes.b: Soap does not work equally well in all water. In hard water it is partly wasted, because ions in the water react with it.
points: Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, for example water from limestone regions.
These ions react with soap ions to form an insoluble scum (a solid that does not dissolve): 2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻(aq) + Ca²⁺(aq) → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca(s).
In hard water, soap forms scum and lathers poorly until all the hardness ions have been precipitated (removed as solid), which wastes soap.
In deionised, soft water (water with the ions removed), soap lathers easily.
notes.tip: The hardness ions are Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, not Na⁺. Exams ask what you see when soap is shaken with deionised water (lather) and with hard water (scum, little lather). Measuring hardness by EDTA titration is not on the specification.

notes.h: Synthetic detergents and types of surfactant
notes.b: Chemists solved the scum problem by changing the head of the surfactant. Surfactants can then be sorted into groups by the charge on that head.
points: Synthetic detergents, also called soapless detergents, have a similar head-and-tail structure but a different head, e.g. a sulfonate group (–SO₃⁻) in alkylbenzene sulfonates.
Their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble, so synthetic detergents work well in hard water and form no scum.
Surfactants are grouped by their head: anionic (negative head), e.g. soaps and sulfonates in washing-up liquid and laundry detergent.
Cationic surfactants have a positive head, e.g. quaternary ammonium compounds in fabric conditioners and some disinfectants.
Non-ionic surfactants have an uncharged head and are used in many cleaning products.
notes.tip: If asked why synthetic detergents do not form scum in hard water, say that their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble.

notes.b: Any job that needs oil and water to mix, or a liquid to spread over a surface, uses a surfactant. The uses fall into four groups.
points: Cleaning: bar and liquid soaps, hand wash, shower gel, shampoo, washing-up liquid, laundry detergent, and household and industrial surface cleaners.
Personal care: toothpaste, where sodium lauryl sulfate is the foaming agent; shampoo; and cosmetics and creams, where surfactants act as emulsifiers (substances that keep oil and water mixed).
Food: emulsifiers such as lecithin, a natural emulsifier from soya or egg yolk, keep oil and water mixed in mayonnaise, chocolate and margarine.

Other uses: fabric conditioners; wetting agents (substances that help a liquid spread over a surface) in paints, inks and agricultural sprays, so that the spray spreads over leaves; firefighting foams; and dispersants that break up oil spills at sea.
notes.tip: Exams ask for applications of surfactants. Give specific uses, such as those above, rather than just saying cleaning.

notes.b: Surfactants have made a major contribution to public health, because they remove microorganisms and the grease that shelters them.
points: Handwashing with soap removes microorganisms from the skin, trapping them in micelles that are rinsed away.
Handwashing is one of the most effective ways of preventing the spread of infectious diseases such as diarrhoeal diseases, respiratory infections and influenza.

Soap destroys enveloped viruses (viruses with a fatty outer layer), such as influenza viruses and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19: the hydrophobic tails insert into the virus's fatty lipid outer membrane and break it apart.
Public-health advice during the COVID-19 pandemic was to wash hands with soap and water, scrubbing for at least 20 seconds.
Detergents used in laundry, dishwashing, hospitals and food processing remove the grease that shelters bacteria, improving hygiene in homes, hospitals and the food industry.
notes.tip: To outline how surfactants have improved health and sanitation, pick two points from handwashing removing microorganisms, soap destroying enveloped viruses, and detergents removing grease that shelters bacteria.

notes.b: Surfactants also caused pollution problems, and the solutions show how detergent design changed. These facts belong here only as impacts of surfactant use.
points: Early synthetic detergents with branched hydrocarbon chains were not biodegradable (microorganisms could not break them down), so they caused foam on rivers in the 1950s and 1960s; they were replaced by biodegradable linear-chain detergents.

Phosphates added to some detergents as builders (additives that improve cleaning) can cause eutrophication (over-enrichment with nutrients) of lakes and rivers, so their use has been restricted, e.g. in laundry detergents in the EU.
The EU restricted phosphates in household laundry detergents from 2013 and in household dishwasher detergents from 2017.

notes.h: Investigation: making soap, aim and chemistry
notes.b: Soap can be made at small scale from kitchen materials. The reaction splits a fat or oil into soap and glycerol using sodium hydroxide.
points: Aim: to make soap on a small scale from household reactants, by base hydrolysis (saponification, the splitting of a fat or oil by an alkali) with sodium hydroxide, and to compare the product when sodium hydroxide is limiting with when it is in excess.
Word equation: fat or oil + sodium hydroxide gives soap (the sodium salts of fatty acids) + glycerol.
One mole of fat reacts with 3 moles of NaOH, because each fat molecule has three ester links to break.
Household reactants: a vegetable oil or fat, e.g. olive, sunflower or coconut oil, or lard; sodium hydroxide, sold as caustic soda; water; and table salt for brine (concentrated salt solution).
A reflux method (boiling with a condenser fitted to return the vapour) is not required: the mixture is heated gently in an open container in a water bath.
notes.tip: Don't present reflux as the required method. Exams ask for the reactants and the co-product of soap-making, and for the structure of glycerol.

notes.b: The method has two halves: making the soap by heating, then separating it from the other products with brine and washing.
points: 1. Weigh a known mass of oil, e.g. 10 g, into a beaker or evaporating basin.

2. Add a measured volume of sodium hydroxide solution of known concentration; a little ethanol, if available, can be added as a solvent in which both the oil and the sodium hydroxide dissolve, so that they mix and react faster.
3. Heat gently in a water bath, stirring continuously, for about 20–30 minutes, adding a little water if the mixture dries out; the mixture becomes thick and creamy as soap forms.

4. Pour the mixture into a beaker of saturated salt solution (brine) and stir; the soap separates as solid curds, because soap is much less soluble in concentrated salt solution than in water; this is salting out.
5. Collect the soap by filtration or by skimming it off, and wash it with a little ice-cold water, because warm water would dissolve the soap.
6. Press the soap dry between filter papers, leave it to dry and weigh it.
7. Repeat with the same mass of oil but a different amount of sodium hydroxide, so that one batch has NaOH in excess and the other has NaOH limiting (the calculation block works an example).
Diagram: a beaker of oil and sodium hydroxide solution in a water bath, with a stirring rod and a thermometer, and a filter funnel collecting the soap from the brine.
notes.tip: Wash with ice-cold water, not warm. A full description of the activity includes the purpose of the brine and of washing the soap with ice-cold water.

notes.b: Simple tests show whether the product behaves like soap and how the amount of sodium hydroxide affected it.
points: Shake a little soap with deionised water: it forms a lather, and the solution is slightly alkaline, about pH 9–10.
Shake a little soap with hard water, e.g. mineral water from a limestone region: a scum forms and there is little lather.
Test a solution of each batch with universal indicator or a pH meter: soap made with excess NaOH has a much higher pH, unless the NaOH has been washed out.
Look and feel the soap, wearing gloves: soap from a batch with limiting NaOH is greasy and soft, with an oily layer of unreacted oil.
The glycerol co-product (the second product of the reaction) and any excess sodium hydroxide dissolve in the brine filtrate (the liquid that passes through the filter), not in the washed soap.
notes.tip: Exams ask what is seen when the soap is shaken with deionised water and with hard water, and where the co-product and excess NaOH end up. Glycerol stays in the filtrate, not in the soap.

notes.b: Each choice in the method has a reason, and exam questions ask for it directly.
points: Heating speeds up the hydrolysis (the splitting of the fat by water and alkali), which is slow at room temperature; a water bath gives gentle, even heat and avoids a flame, because ethanol is flammable.
Stirring mixes the oil with the aqueous sodium hydroxide (sodium hydroxide dissolved in water), which do not mix by themselves, so they keep reacting.
Brine separates the soap from glycerol, water and excess NaOH, which all stay in solution.
Washing with ice-cold water removes NaOH and glycerol from the soap surface without dissolving much soap.
notes.tip: Exams ask why brine is added and why the soap is washed, and with what. Say that brine makes the soap separate while the other substances stay dissolved, and wash with ice-cold water.

notes.b: Sodium hydroxide is the main hazard in this activity. The errors listed below also explain why the mass of soap you get is not exact.
points: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive and especially harmful to the eyes: wear goggles and gloves.
Add the sodium hydroxide carefully, because dissolving NaOH in water is exothermic (it gives out heat).
Do not use the product on skin, because it may contain unreacted sodium hydroxide.
Sources of error include soap lost in the brine and washings, wet soap being weighed, which gives too high a mass, and a reaction not completed in the time allowed.
Household oils are mixtures, so the mass of NaOH needed can only be estimated.

notes.h: Consequences of limiting or excess sodium hydroxide (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A reagent is limiting when it runs out first and so sets how much product forms. Whether the sodium hydroxide or the fat runs out first changes the quality of the soap.
points: If NaOH is limiting, not all the fat is hydrolysed: the yield of soap is set by the moles of NaOH, and unreacted fat or oil remains.
The soap made with limiting NaOH is greasy and soft, and the leftover oil is wasted and can go rancid (turn foul-smelling and spoiled).
If NaOH is in excess, all the fat is converted, giving the maximum yield of soap from the fat.
The soap made with excess NaOH contains free sodium hydroxide, which is caustic, has a high pH and irritates or burns skin.
Excess NaOH must be removed, by washing the soap with brine or water, or by neutralisation (reacting it with an acid).
Excess NaOH is also wasted reagent and makes the waste liquid strongly alkaline.
notes.tip: Excess NaOH means the maximum soap from the fat but caustic soap; limiting NaOH means less soap and leftover fat. Don't say excess NaOH gives more soap than the fat allows.

notes.h: How soap makers deal with NaOH amounts (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Because both too little and too much sodium hydroxide cause problems, soap makers work out the amount carefully.
points: Manufacturers calculate the exact amount of NaOH needed for the fat used, then wash the soap with brine to remove any excess.
Small-scale soap makers often use slightly less NaOH than needed, leaving a little unreacted oil, called superfatting, so that no free NaOH remains and the soap is gentler.
The amount of NaOH needed follows from the 1 : 3 ratio of fat to NaOH; for a real oil it can only be estimated, because oils are mixtures of different tri-esters (molecules with three ester links).
notes.tip: A question on consequences usually also asks how manufacturers deal with them: calculate the exact NaOH, then wash with brine.

notes.b: This worked example uses sample data and a model fat to find the soap made when NaOH is in excess and when it is limiting. Remember that the fat reacts with NaOH in a 1 : 3 mole ratio.
points: Model fat: glyceryl tristearate, M = 890 g mol⁻¹; sodium stearate (soap), M = 306 g mol⁻¹; NaOH, M = 40 g mol⁻¹. Sample data.
8.90 g of fat = 8.90 ÷ 890 = 0.0100 mol, which needs 3 × 0.0100 = 0.0300 mol of NaOH = 1.20 g.
Batch 1, NaOH in excess: 2.00 g of NaOH = 0.0500 mol; 0.0300 mol reacts, leaving 0.0200 mol (0.800 g) over. The fat is limiting, so soap = 3 × 0.0100 = 0.0300 mol × 306 = 9.18 g.
Batch 2, NaOH limiting: 1.00 g of NaOH = 0.0250 mol, less than the 0.0300 mol needed. Soap = 0.0250 mol × 306 = 7.65 g.
In batch 2, fat used = 0.0250 ÷ 3 = 0.00833 mol, so fat left unreacted = 0.0100 − 0.00833 = 0.001667 mol; keep the extra figure until the end, then 0.001667 × 890 = 1.48 g.
Conclusion: batch 1 gives more soap, 9.18 g, but contains 0.800 g of corrosive NaOH that must be washed out; batch 2 gives less soap, 7.65 g, mixed with 1.48 g of unreacted fat.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the maximum mass of soap from a given mass of fat. To find which reagent is limiting, convert both masses to moles and compare them using the 1 : 3 ratio.

keyTerms.definition: A substance whose molecules have a hydrophilic part and a hydrophobic part, which lowers the surface tension of water.
The sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid, which acts as a surfactant.
Attracted to water, as in the ionic carboxylate head of a soap ion.
Repelled by water and attracted to grease, as in the hydrocarbon tail of a soap ion.
A sphere of surfactant ions with their hydrophobic tails inside, holding grease or oil droplets, with their hydrophilic heads facing the water.
A mixture of two liquids that do not mix, in which one liquid is dispersed as tiny droplets in the other.
An insoluble solid formed when soap ions react with Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺ ions in hard water.
A surfactant made from petrochemicals that does not form scum in hard water, because its calcium and magnesium salts are soluble.
Able to be broken down by microorganisms into simple substances.
The base hydrolysis of a fat or oil by sodium hydroxide, which gives soap and glycerol.
The separation of soap from its solution by adding concentrated salt solution, in which soap is much less soluble.
The common name for sodium hydroxide, NaOH.
Propane-1,2,3-triol, HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH, the co-product of making soap from a fat.
The reactant that is used up first and so limits the amount of product that can form.
A reactant present in more than the amount needed, so some of it is left over at the end of the reaction.
Making soap with slightly less sodium hydroxide than needed, so that a little unreacted oil remains and no free NaOH is left.

questions.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a labelled diagram, how soap removes grease from skin. Use the terms hydrophilic, hydrophobic and micelle.
questions.model: A soap ion has a hydrophilic head, the –COO⁻ group, which is ionic and attracted to water, and a hydrophobic tail, a long hydrocarbon chain that is attracted to grease. In water, soap lowers the surface tension so the water wets the greasy skin. The hydrophobic tails dissolve in the grease while the hydrophilic heads stay in the water. Rubbing breaks the grease into small droplets, each surrounded by soap ions. Each droplet becomes a micelle, with the tails pointing inwards into the grease and the negatively charged heads pointing outwards into the water. The negative charges on the micelles repel one another, so they stay dispersed as an emulsion, and rinsing carries them away. The diagram should show a micelle with an oil droplet in the centre, tails pointing inward, and heads on the outside in water.

questions.prompt: Explain why soap forms a scum in hard water, giving an equation, and why synthetic detergents do not. Give two everyday applications of surfactants other than washing hands.
questions.model: Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, which react with soap ions to form an insoluble scum: 2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻(aq) + Ca²⁺(aq) → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca(s). Synthetic detergents have sulfonate heads, such as –SO₃⁻ in alkylbenzene sulfonates, and their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble, so no scum forms. Two applications, from any of: toothpaste, where sodium lauryl sulfate is a foaming agent; shampoo; cosmetics and creams, where surfactants are emulsifiers; lecithin in mayonnaise or margarine; fabric conditioners; paint and spray wetting agents; firefighting foams; dispersants for oil spills.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which surfactants have contributed to the health and sanitation of society.
questions.model: First, handwashing with soap removes microorganisms from the skin in micelles, which are rinsed away, and it is one of the most effective ways of preventing the spread of infectious diseases such as diarrhoeal diseases, respiratory infections and influenza. Second, soap destroys enveloped viruses such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2, because its hydrophobic tails insert into the virus's fatty outer membrane and break it apart. Detergents used in hospitals and food processing also remove grease that shelters bacteria.

questions.prompt: Describe a simple activity to make a small sample of soap from vegetable oil and sodium hydroxide, explaining the purpose of the brine and of washing the soap with ice-cold water.
questions.model: Weigh about 10 g of vegetable oil into a beaker and add a measured volume of sodium hydroxide solution, with a little ethanol if available to help the two mix. Heat gently in a water bath for 20 to 30 minutes, stirring continuously and adding a little water if the mixture dries out; the mixture becomes thick and creamy as soap forms. Pour the mixture into saturated salt solution, the brine, and stir. The soap separates as solid curds, because soap is much less soluble in concentrated salt solution, and the brine keeps the glycerol, water and excess sodium hydroxide in solution, separating them from the soap. Filter the soap, and wash it with a little ice-cold water: the cold water removes sodium hydroxide and glycerol from the surface, whereas warm water would dissolve the soap. Press the soap dry, leave it to dry and weigh it. Wear goggles and gloves, because sodium hydroxide is corrosive.

questions.prompt: Explain the consequences for the soap produced of using (i) too little sodium hydroxide, (ii) too much sodium hydroxide, and state how manufacturers deal with this.
questions.model: (i) Too little sodium hydroxide means it is limiting. Not all the fat is hydrolysed, so the yield of soap is set by the moles of NaOH, and unreacted fat or oil remains, making the soap greasy and soft. (ii) Too much sodium hydroxide means it is in excess. All the fat is converted, giving the maximum yield of soap, but the soap contains free sodium hydroxide, which is caustic, has a high pH and irritates or burns skin, and the excess is wasted. Manufacturers calculate the exact amount of NaOH needed for the fat and then wash the soap with brine to remove any excess. Small-scale soap makers may use slightly less NaOH than needed, leaving a little unreacted oil, which is called superfatting, so that no free NaOH remains.

questions.prompt: 4.45 g of glyceryl tristearate (M = 890) was heated with 0.400 g of sodium hydroxide. Show which reagent is limiting and calculate the maximum mass of sodium stearate (M = 306) that could form (sample data).
questions.model: Moles of fat = 4.45 ÷ 890 = 0.00500 mol. NaOH needed for complete reaction = 3 × 0.00500 = 0.0150 mol. Moles of NaOH available = 0.400 ÷ 40 = 0.0100 mol, which is less than 0.0150 mol, so the NaOH is limiting. Soap formed = 0.0100 mol × 306 = 3.06 g, since 3 mol of NaOH give 3 mol of soap. Fat used = 0.0100 ÷ 3 = 0.00333 mol, so unreacted fat = (0.00500 − 0.00333) × 890 = 0.001667 × 890 = 1.48 g.
